**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More, or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two of our internal tools have started timing out intermittently. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy another node or find a way to squeeze more out of what we already own. I want to lay out my thinking on this before we commit either way, because the decision is less symmetric than it first appears.

The case for buying is straightforward. Hardware is a known quantity: we know the vendor, we know the lead time, we know roughly what it costs, and we know it will work the day it arrives. Adding capacity is the fastest way to make the pain go away, and pain that shows up in user-facing latency is pain that erodes trust in the tools we've built. Every time the batch service stalls, someone quietly goes back to doing that work by hand, and winning them back is harder than never losing them.

But the case for improving utilisation deserves more credit than it usually gets. Our telemetry suggests our fleet sits at roughly 35–40% average utilisation, with peaks that spike past 90%. That gap is the signature of a scheduling problem, not a capacity problem. Our models are loaded eagerly at startup whether or not they're needed that hour; our batch jobs and interactive traffic share a naive first-come queue; and we have no mechanism for preemption, so a long-running fine-tune can block latency-sensitive requests for an hour. If we implemented proper model swapping, priority queues, and time-shifting batch work into the overnight window, I believe we could effectively double our usable capacity without spending a dollar on silicon. The engineering cost is real — call it three to four weeks of focused work from one or two people — but that's a fraction of the capital cost of a new node, and unlike hardware, that work compounds: better scheduling discipline pays off on every future machine we ever own.

There's also the question of what we give up by buying. Capital spent on a node is capital not spent on hiring, on tooling, or on the evaluation work we've been deferring. And hardware is a largely irreversible commitment. If our workload mix shifts — if a vendor API gets cheaper, if a project gets cancelled, if a model gets small enough to run on commodity CPUs — a purchased node becomes shelfware that we'll feel obligated to justify. Scheduling improvements, by contrast, are almost perfectly reversible. If they don't deliver, we've lost a few weeks of engineering time and learned something about our own traffic patterns that we'd need to know anyway before any purchase.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about that. Right now, a single node failure takes down a meaningful share of our capacity, and buying a second node would genuinely improve our redundancy posture. That argument has real weight. But redundancy bought through utilisation improvements is partial at best — if we're running everything at 80% on one node, we haven't reduced our blast radius. My answer is that we should treat reliability as a separate, smaller purchase: not a full node, but perhaps a single mid-range card as a hot spare, which addresses the failure-mode concern at maybe a fifth of the cost.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next six weeks on utilisation work — dynamic model loading, priority scheduling, batch off-peak migration — and simultaneously price out a modest spare card for redundancy. Revisit the full-node question at the end of that window with real data in hand. If utilisation work gets us to a sustainable place, we've saved the money. If it doesn't, we'll buy the node knowing exactly what our true headroom is, which makes us far better negotiators and far better planners.

The uncertainty here is genuine. My utilisation estimates come from coarse instrumentation, and it's possible the real ceiling is lower than I think. But that's precisely the argument for measuring before buying: the cost of finding out is a few weeks of engineering time, while the cost of guessing wrong is a capital purchase we can't undo. I'd rather be surprised cheaply than expensively.

Happy to walk through the telemetry in our next sync. Please send objections or counterarguments before Friday so we can lock in a plan.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI hardware investment decision
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've hit the point where our inference cluster is visibly strained. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, the on-call rotation has fielded two capacity-related incidents, and several of you have asked, reasonably, whether we should just buy more hardware. I've spent time with the utilisation data, the vendor quotes, and our own incident history, and I want to lay out my thinking before we commit either way. My recommendation is that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and defer the purchase decision until we have evidence that we genuinely need it.

The case for buying more is the obvious one: it works. Capacity problems are stressful, and adding machines makes the stress go away quickly. But the vendor quote we received is substantial — roughly the equivalent of two full-time engineers for a year — and that money buys us hardware that will depreciate whether or not we use it well. More importantly, it buys us a decision we can't easily undo. Once the purchase is approved and the machines are racked, that capital is spent. If our workload shifts, if a hosted API becomes materially cheaper, or if we simply overestimated demand, we're stuck with sunk cost and a rack of equipment we're reluctant to decommission because it was expensive. Reversibility matters more than it first appears. The alternative path — squeezing more out of what we own — is almost entirely reversible. If we tune batching, right-size our model deployments, and fix the scheduling gaps, and utilisation still isn't enough, we can buy hardware then with much better information. Nothing is wasted; the tuning work pays dividends regardless.

And there is a lot of headroom. Our telemetry shows average GPU utilisation across the cluster sitting near thirty percent, with sharp peaks that drive our queue-time complaints. That pattern is classic for a fleet serving bursty, interactive traffic with static allocation. Batched inference, dynamic model loading so we're not pinning large models to idle GPUs, and a smarter queue that prioritises latency-sensitive requests should, based on comparable efforts elsewhere, recover a large fraction of that idle capacity. The engineering cost is real — I'd estimate four to six weeks of focused work from two of us — but it's labour we'd likely spend anyway on operational hygiene, and it builds capability (better observability, better scheduling) that makes any future purchase smaller and smarter.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to be honest about it. If our product direction pushes toward real-time, interactive AI features where sub-second response is a hard requirement, then aggressive batching and dynamic loading can trade away tail latency in ways that are painful to debug. Buying hardware is the low-risk answer for latency guarantees. My view is that we don't yet know whether that's our direction. The product roadmap is genuinely uncertain, and committing capital to serve a latency profile we may not need is exactly the kind of bet we should defer until the requirements firm up. If interactive features do become central, we can revisit this with a much clearer picture.

Reliability cuts both ways. Right now, a single node failure during peak load degrades service noticeably, and more hardware would add redundancy. But our recent incidents were as much about configuration and scheduling as raw capacity, and a well-instrumented, well-scheduled fleet of existing machines is more reliable than a larger fleet we don't understand. Utilisation work directly improves reliability; a purchase only improves it indirectly.

The opportunity cost is the final consideration. The money for new hardware could fund a second engineer, a hosted-inference pilot, or simply extend our runway. Those alternatives are not free of risk either — hosted APIs introduce vendor dependency and per-token costs that grow with usage — but they keep options open in a way that a capital purchase does not.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty in my own position. Utilisation projections are notoriously optimistic, and it's possible we'll do the work, recover less capacity than hoped, and end up buying hardware in six months having spent effort along the way. I think that's an acceptable cost. The downside of buying now and being wrong is larger and less recoverable.

**Recommendation:** Approve a one-quarter utilisation initiative with explicit success metrics — target average utilisation above sixty percent and p95 queue times under five seconds. Revisit the purchase decision in Q3 with real data. If we miss those targets, we buy, and we'll do so knowing exactly what we need and why.

Happy to walk through the telemetry in detail on Thursday.
